segments: The Chronography of Bar Hebraeus.
And they sent to Saladin that they would surrender it to him.
The Sultan, however, sent his nephew and his cousin so that it might be surrendered to them.
The guards, however, were not willing,
until Saladin himself went in person and took possession of it.
And to those who had surrendered it he gave gifts,
and he led them out of the fortress.
And to that governor,
he did no harm,
because the nobles helped him and said
that the guards had lied about him.
Then Saladin placed his son al-Malik al-Zahir in the fortress of Aleppo,
and he himself went to Damascus.
And from there he gathered an army, and went and encamped against the fortress of Kerak,
and waged a fierce battle against it.
The Franks, however, gathered together and wanted to attack him.
And when he became aware of it,
he left Kerak and returned to Damascus.
And his brother, Malik Adil, came to him from Egypt,
and brought him much gold.
And he made him governor over Aleppo and its territory (and its district),
as far as Ra'ban and the banks of the Euphrates,
[and] as far as Hamah.
And Adil entered the fortress of Aleppo,
and al-Zahir, the son of Saladin, went out after having been in it for six months,
and he went to his father.
And in the year one thousand four hundred and ninety-five [of the Greeks],
[that is] 580 of the Arabs,
Saladin prepared for war against Kerak.
And he sent and brought Nur al-Din from Hisn Kayfa,
and his brother Adil from Aleppo,
and Taqi al-Din from Egypt,
and they all assembled against Kerak.
The Franks, however, gathered together again,
and the Turks were shaken.
And Saladin gave orders, and they burned the mangonels that they had erected against Kerak,
and they abandoned [the siege] and went to the district of Samaria and plundered it.
Prince Reynald, however, the lord of Kerak, went by way of the mountains,
and entered Kerak,
and fortified it further.
And the Prince, the lord of Antioch, also went out to Harim with two hundred horsemen,
and took plunder from the country,
and killed many of the Arab horsemen who were stationed at the bridge called the Iron Bridge.
And the Franks also overcame an ambush of the Arabs on the mountain,
four hundred infantry and twenty horsemen,
and they killed them all.
